newsitem.title: USA: Not much room for more heating oil at U.S. refiners.
newsitem.headline: Not much room for more heating oil at U.S. refiners.

text.p: While heating oil stocks are at historically low levels, refiners and oil industry analysts said Monday there was little extra capacity for boosting inventories in time for winter.

"The notion that refiners can be coaxed into producing more distillate is off base. The flexibility just isn't there," said Charles McSpadden, vice president of market analysis at Bonner & Moore. Distillates are oil products that include heating oil.
On Friday, the Department of Energy said it would ask oil executives if there was extra refining capacity to produce additional heating oil to help build up low East Coast stocks.
Inventories on the East Coast, the world's largest heating oil market, are 43 percent below year-ago levels.

Late on Friday, Tosco Corp. pledged to maximize distillate production at its Bayway refinery in Linden, N.J. But refiners such as Texaco Inc. and Amoco Corp. said Monday they were already running full-tilt.
Even if there are no shortages, consumers are likely to face higher prices this winter than last.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration is predicting average heating oil prices this winter will be 9 cents a gallon higher than last winter, although the current retail price of $1.11 is 20 cents higher than a year ago.
At any rate, it would be difficult for refiners to build up stocks significantly before winter, analysts said.

"U.S. refiners are up (running) at historical high levels for this time of year. There is not much room to produce more," said an analyst consulting for the federal government on the heating oil crisis.
The analyst said refiners were already producing between 200,000 to 300,000 barrels per day more of distillates, with much of the production in the Gulf Coast.
"The Gulf Coast is an important incremental location to generate supplies for the East Coast," said the analyst.
Delays in scheduled refinery maintenance may also not be as long as originally hoped, since many refiners have contractual commitments with construction crews, said the analyst.
Bonner & Moore's McSpadden pointed out that most refiners can only delay two to three months because of safety and weather concerns, which means the crunch may be felt later in the winter.
"You can delay (maintenance) only for so long," said McSpadden.
Both analysts added that the amount of distillate that can be captured out of a barrel of crude is also running at historically high levels.
In September, distillate production was about 21.1 percent of the crude barrel, and 22.5 percent was forecast for October. Both are highs that have not been seen the Gulf War, said the consultant.
Pushing more crude through the system is also impractical, since about 50 percent of the barrel yields gasoline, which might have to go into costly storage during fall and winter.
"Refinery economics revolves around the total economics of the barrel," said McSpadden. "The bottom line is there is not that much flexibility.
"But that doesn't necessarily indicate a severe shortfall, it's just going to be a firm price."

McSpadden forecasts stocks will slowly begin to creep up to last year's level of about 125 million barrels in the fourth quarter. He predicted imports in the quarter would average about 240,000 barrels a day, which compares with 219,000 barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 1995.
"That's really where I think the markets satisfactory incremental demand will come from," he said, referring to imports.
